newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Marines fired radioactive bullets near Okinawa.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Marines fired radioactive bullets near Okinawa.

text.p: U.S. Marine Corp jets accidentally fired 1,520 bullets containing depleted uranium during a military exercise on an island near Okinawa, Japan in late 1995 and early 1996, the Washington Times reported on Monday.

A U.S. Defence Department spokesman confirmed the incident and said the bullets had been mislabeled as "armor piercing" bullets. He said an expert U.S. team had assessed the environmental and health impact of the accidental use of the radioactive bullets and found there were no health or environmental risks.
A U.S. contractor recovered 192 of the bullets during a March 1996 cleanup, the newspaper said, quoting Dan Boyd, a U.S. Air Force spokesman in Japan.

The level of radioactivity measured on Tori Shima, an isolated gunnery range 54 miles (87 km) from Okinawa, was reported to be 10 times less than the level under which the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission would require a cleanup plan.

The Washington Times said the Pentagon only notified Japan about the incident last month, but the spokesman said the U.S. government was not required to notify the Japanese unless there were any health risks.
A decision was made to notify Japan anyway after a press inquiry about the incident, the spokesman said.
"The amounts we are talking about here are absolutely insignificant," the spokesman said, adding that the radioactivity given off by the bullets was similar to that of early television sets.
The spokesman said the ammunition was intended for use only in combat or live-fire exercises in the United States. No nuclear ammunition was to be used on Okinawa under a U.S.-Japanese agreement.

The newspaper quoted military officials as saying that the bullets were classified as conventional, not nuclear, weaponry. Each of the 25 mm shells fired contained 5.2 ounces (147 gm) of depleted uranium, a heavy metal with about the same toxicity as lead, the newspaper reported.
Okinawa was the scene of bloody fighting during the Second World War and was occupied by U.S. forces until 1972, when it returned to Japanese control.
